entry.title: The Segfault That Passed Code Review
entry.summary: How a stale Conan profile in our Bazel monorepo turned std::filesystem::path into a ticking time bomb.
entry.content:
How a Conan profile still set to libstdc++ in a libstdc++11 monorepo turned every std::filesystem::path crossing a library boundary into a silent memory-layout disagreement, and why the segfault took weeks to find.

The crash

$ bazel test //services/ingest:config_parser_test
...
Signal: SIGSEGV (Segmentation fault)

No assertion failed. No sanitizer fired during the build. Just a clean segfault, not in a complex computation or a file operation, but in a destructor:

void ConfigParser::loadFrom() {
    std::unique_ptr<std::filesystem::path> config_path(
        static_cast<std::filesystem::path*>(
            configlib_create_path("/usr/share/config/app.conf")  // extern "C"
        )
    );

    std::ifstream file(config_path->c_str());
    // ... parse configuration ...
}   // <-- SIGSEGV here, when unique_ptr runs the destructor

The path string was valid. The file was opened and read successfully. The crash came at scope exit, when the unique_ptr ran the destructor on a perfectly ordinary-looking path object. Nothing about the code itself explained a crash, and nothing in the code review two weeks earlier had raised a flag. That's because the bug wasn't in the code. It was in how the code was built.

A field that wasn't there

The backtrace was short and pointed deep inside the standard library:

#0  std::filesystem::__cxx11::path::_List::_Impl_deleter::operator()() ()
       from /lib/x86_64-linux-gnu/libstdc++.so.6
#1  std::filesystem::__cxx11::path::_List::~_List() ()
#2  std::filesystem::__cxx11::path::~path() ()
#3  ConfigParser::loadFrom() ()
       at config_parser.cpp:47

The crash was inside ~path(). C++ destroys members in reverse declaration order, so the destructor started with the last member: _M_cmpts, the parsed-component storage. In the new ABI, _M_cmpts sits at offset +32 inside the path object. But the library had built a 16-byte old-ABI path. Offset +32 was 16 bytes past the end of the actual object. The destructor read whatever happened to be in adjacent memory, interpreted it as a unique_ptr<_Impl> (a pointer to the component storage implementation), and tried to dereference it. The value there was 0x1a — unmapped memory. SIGSEGV.

In GDB, a raw dump of the memory at the path pointer showed what was happening:

(gdb) x/5gx config_path
0x55a3e890:  0x000055a3e8c8  0x000055a3e8f0
0x55a3e8a0:  0x0000000000000000  0x0000000000000041
0x55a3e8b0:  0x000000000000001a

The first two quadwords (16 bytes) were the actual path object: a COW data pointer and the old-ABI _M_cmpts. Everything after was outside the object — heap metadata and the start of the string's COW control block. The value at offset +32, 0x1a (26 decimal), was the COW block's _M_length field — literally the string length of "/usr/share/config/app.conf". The new-ABI destructor read that string length as a pointer and tried to follow it.

The question shifted from "what's wrong with the code" to "what's wrong with the object."

The sizeof that explained everything

The next diagnostic was crude but decisive:

// Added to the test (compiled with GCC 12, libstdc++11):
std::cerr << "sizeof(path) in test: " << sizeof(std::filesystem::path) << "\n";

// Added to the library that constructs the path (compiled with GCC 8, libstdc++):
std::cerr << "sizeof(path) in lib:  " << sizeof(std::filesystem::path) << "\n";
sizeof(path) in test: 40
sizeof(path) in lib:  16

Forty bytes versus sixteen. The library allocated a 16-byte old-ABI path. When the consumer's unique_ptr went out of scope, it ran the new-ABI destructor, which expected a 40-byte object. The destructor tried to clean up _M_cmpts at offset +32 — 16 bytes past the end of the real object — read garbage from adjacent memory, interpreted it as a pointer, and crashed dereferencing it. That's the crash.

The reason for the size difference is std::string. std::filesystem::path stores its pathname as a std::string internally. And std::string has two different memory layouts in libstdc++, controlled by the _GLIBCXX_USE_CXX11_ABI macro (or, in Conan terms, the compiler.libcxx setting).

The old layout (libstdc++, _GLIBCXX_USE_CXX11_ABI=0) uses copy-on-write (COW) with a single pointer to a heap-allocated control block. The new layout (libstdc++11, _GLIBCXX_USE_CXX11_ABI=1) uses the small string optimization (SSO) with inline storage for short strings:

These are different sizes: 8 bytes versus 32 bytes on x86-64. You cannot hand one to code expecting the other. And since std::filesystem::path contains a std::string, the path inherits the mismatch:

libstdc++ (old) libstdc++11 (new)
_M_pathname (std::string) 8 bytes 32 bytes
_M_cmpts (component storage) 8 bytes 8 bytes
Total sizeof(path) 16 bytes 40 bytes

That explained both the GDB output and the crash. The first 8 bytes of the old-ABI object were a heap pointer, which the new-ABI consumer also interpreted as a heap pointer (both ABIs store a pointer at offset 0). So GDB could read the actual string content. But bytes 8–15 of the old object, the component storage, were interpreted as the string length, producing a nonsensical value in the trillions. And bytes 16–39, which the consumer expected to find, didn't belong to the path object at all. The destructor only needed to read _M_cmpts at offset +32 to crash — the garbage there was a string length (26), which it dereferenced as a pointer to unmapped memory.

Why the linker didn't save us

libstdc++ has a safety mechanism for catching this kind of mismatch. New-ABI types like std::string live in an inline namespace __cxx11, so old-ABI and new-ABI strings mangle differently:

Old ABI:  std::basic_string<char>
New ABI:  std::__cxx11::basic_string<char>

If you try to link a function that takes std::string across the ABI boundary, the linker rejects it with an undefined symbol error. Since GCC 11, std::filesystem::path also lives in the __cxx11 namespace:

Old ABI:  std::filesystem::path
New ABI:  std::filesystem::__cxx11::path

A direct C++ function taking const path& mangles differently between ABIs, and the linker would reject it.

But our Conan library's public API used C-linkage wrappers, a common pattern for packages intended to work across compiler versions. Path objects were returned through extern "C" functions as opaque pointers and cast back to std::filesystem::path* on the consumer side. C linkage strips all C++ type information from the symbol, so the linker saw matching, undecorated symbols on both sides and was satisfied. It had no way to know that the pointer referred to a 16-byte object the consumer would read as 40 bytes.

Link-time success only proves symbol compatibility. It does not prove ABI compatibility. In our case, the binary linked cleanly, ran successfully, and crashed in a destructor.

A profile nobody remembered

With the mechanism understood, the question was: how did an old-ABI library end up in a new-ABI build?

The answer was in Conan. Our monorepo used Conan to manage a handful of external C++ dependencies. One of them, a configuration-file parser, depended on a utility library that exposed std::filesystem::path in its API. The Conan profile used to build and cache these packages:

# conan_profile_legacy
[settings]
os=Linux
compiler=gcc
compiler.version=8
compiler.libcxx=libstdc++
build_type=Release

That compiler.libcxx=libstdc++ is the problem. It tells Conan to build with _GLIBCXX_USE_CXX11_ABI=0: the old, COW-based string layout. The monorepo's own Bazel toolchain used GCC 12 with the default libstdc++11 (new ABI). No one had updated the Conan profile when the monorepo migrated compilers, because no one remembered it existed. The Conan packages were cached in the CI artifact store, built months ago, and just kept working until someone added a code path that passed a std::filesystem::path across the boundary.

The misconfiguration had been latent the entire time. Simpler types like integers, plain structs, and C strings had crossed the C-linkage boundary without issue because their layouts don't change between ABIs. It was only when someone added a code path that passed a std::filesystem::path through the opaque-pointer interface that the layout mismatch became a runtime fault.

What we changed

The immediate fix was one line: update the Conan profile.

# conan_profile (updated)
[settings]
os=Linux
compiler=gcc
compiler.version=12
compiler.libcxx=libstdc++11
build_type=Release

Rebuild and re-cache every Conan package. Segfault gone.

But "update the profile" is a fix for this incident, not for the class of problem. Three things changed to make it harder for this to happen again:

A compile-time ABI canary. A header shared between the Conan packages and the monorepo now checks both the compiler version and the ABI:

#if defined(__GNUC__) && __GNUC__ < 12
#error "This library must be built with GCC 12+ to match the monorepo toolchain."
#endif

#if _GLIBCXX_USE_CXX11_ABI != 1
#error "This library must be built with the C++11 ABI (compiler.libcxx=libstdc++11)."
#endif

This turns a silent runtime segfault into a loud compile-time error.

Profile generation from the toolchain. The Conan profile is now generated from the same toolchain definition that Bazel uses, rather than being a hand-maintained file that can drift.

C types at package boundaries. Where a Conan-provided library needs to exchange paths with the monorepo, the interface now uses const char* rather than std::filesystem::path. The conversion to path happens on the caller's side, in code compiled with the caller's toolchain. This removes path from the ABI surface entirely.

What makes this class of bug hard

Every defense you'd normally rely on is absent:

  • No compiler warning. Both sides compile cleanly. The mismatch is between translation units that never see each other's source.
  • No linker error. The __cxx11 inline namespace catches ABI mismatches for types like std::string and std::filesystem::path in direct C++ function signatures. It cannot help when objects cross the boundary through C linkage, dlopen, or type erasure.
  • No sanitizer catch (by default). ASan and UBSan instrument a single build. They don't detect layout disagreements between separately compiled artifacts unless you rebuild everything under a single, consistent toolchain, which is exactly the thing that wasn't happening.
  • The crash is non-local. The segfault occurs in the consumer, not in the producer. The library that built the wrong-layout object runs fine; it's the code that reads the object under the wrong assumptions that dies.

And even beyond the libstdc++ / libstdc++11 flag: std::filesystem::path is not ABI-stable across libstdc++ versions at all. Its internal representation (the component storage, the parsing logic, the helper types) changed between GCC 8 and GCC 9 when the implementation moved from the separate libstdc++fs static library into the main libstdc++.so, and continued to evolve through GCC 11 and 12. Types like std::string and std::vector were explicitly frozen after the ABI transition, but std::filesystem::path, std::regex, and other newer types were not part of that freeze.

If your build system consumes prebuilt C++ binaries through Conan, vcpkg, system packages, or anything else, both the libcxx setting and the compiler version are load-bearing. Every unfrozen standard library type you expose across that boundary is a bet that both sides were built with the same libstdc++. When the bet is wrong, nothing tells you until a destructor reads a string length as a pointer and segfaults.

Reproduction

A self-contained reproduction of this crash is available in the example implementation repo.

For a byte-level walkthrough of what happens in memory when the two ABI layouts collide, see the companion article: ABI Mismatch Under the Hood.

entry.title: ABI Mismatch Under the Hood
entry.summary: A byte-level walkthrough of how std::filesystem::path's memory layout differs between GCC ABI versions, and exactly why reading one layout as the other causes a segfault.
entry.content:
This is a companion to The Segfault That Passed Code Review. That article covers the debugging story and the Conan profile that caused it. This one goes deeper into the mechanics: what the compiler bakes into your binary, how the memory layouts differ byte by byte, and exactly what goes wrong when the two meet at runtime.

How std::filesystem is linked

std::filesystem didn't always live where it does today. Its home in libstdc++ shifted between GCC 8 and GCC 9, and that shift matters for understanding what the runtime expects.

GCC 8: The filesystem implementation shipped in a separate static library. You had to link it explicitly:

g++ -std=c++17 main.cpp -lstdc++fs

libstdc++fs.a was a static archive. When you linked against it, the compiled filesystem routines (including parent_path(), filename(), and the parser) were copied directly into your binary. Your executable carried its own private copy of the implementation, baked in at link time.

GCC 9 and later: The implementation moved into the main shared library, libstdc++.so. No extra flag needed:

g++ -std=c++17 main.cpp    # links libstdc++.so automatically

The filesystem routines now live alongside std::string, std::vector, and everything else in the same shared library your binary loads at startup.

This transition matters. With GCC 8, the implementation of parent_path() lives in your binary, compiled when you compiled, with whatever ABI flags you used. With GCC 9+, parent_path() lives in the shared library on the system, compiled once with the ABI that the system's libstdc++ was built with. If your binary creates a path object with one ABI and then hands it to a libstdc++.so that was built with a different ABI, the two sides disagree on the object's memory layout. That disagreement is the root cause of the crash.

What happens when you create a path object

When you write this:

std::filesystem::path p("/usr/share/config/app.conf");

several things are decided at compile time, before the program ever runs.

The header defines the layout

The compiler reads the <filesystem> header, which includes bits/fs_path.h. That header contains the class definition for std::filesystem::path. Stripped to the essentials:

// Simplified from bits/fs_path.h
class path {
    // ...
private:
    std::string  _M_pathname;   // the full path as a string
    _List        _M_cmpts;      // parsed path components
};

From this definition the compiler determines the exact byte-level layout of the type: total size, offset of every field, alignment requirements. Not an approximation, but the precise numbers that will appear as constants in the generated machine code.

Since path contains a std::string as its first member, the layout of path depends on the layout of std::string. And std::string has two layouts in libstdc++, controlled by the _GLIBCXX_USE_CXX11_ABI macro:

  • Old ABI (_GLIBCXX_USE_CXX11_ABI=0): std::string is 8 bytes: a single pointer to a heap-allocated control block that stores the length, capacity, reference count, and character data together (copy-on-write).
  • New ABI (_GLIBCXX_USE_CXX11_ABI=1): std::string is 32 bytes: a pointer, a length, and a union holding either a 16-byte inline character buffer or a capacity value (small-string optimization).

Which layout the compiler uses depends entirely on which ABI flag was active when the header was parsed. The same header, the same field names, two completely different memory layouts.

The layout is baked into your binary

This is the critical point. The compiler does not generate code that asks "how big is std::filesystem::path?" at runtime. It already knows. The size is a compile-time constant, fixed the moment the header was parsed.

Every operation the compiler generates (stack frame allocation, field access, copying, passing by reference) uses hardcoded offsets derived from the header. If the header said _M_cmpts is at offset 32 (because the string before it occupies 32 bytes in the new ABI), then every access to _M_cmpts in your binary will read from start_of_object + 32. That offset is a literal number in the machine code. It will never change at runtime.

The constructor and destructor work the same way. They are defined in the header and typically inlined by the compiler. Your binary contains the constructor code that initializes each field at its expected offset, and the destructor code that tears down each field at its expected offset. Both are hardcoded to the layout the compiler saw.

This means your binary doesn't just know how big a path object is. It knows exactly how to create one and how to destroy one, using the layout that was determined at compile time. If a different binary was compiled with different ABI flags, it will create and destroy path objects using a different layout, and neither binary has any way to detect the mismatch at runtime.

Two compilers, two layouts

With that background, here is what concretely differs between a path object compiled with the old ABI and the new ABI.

Old ABI: GCC 8, _GLIBCXX_USE_CXX11_ABI=0

Offset   Size   Field
──────   ────   ──────────────────────────
  +0      8     _M_pathname  (COW pointer → heap block)
  +8      8     _M_cmpts     (component storage)
──────
 16 bytes total

_M_pathname is a single 8-byte pointer. All the string metadata (length, capacity, and reference count) and the character data itself live in a single heap-allocated block that the pointer references.

New ABI: GCC 12, _GLIBCXX_USE_CXX11_ABI=1

Offset   Size   Field
──────   ────   ──────────────────────────
  +0      8     _M_pathname.ptr      (pointer to char data)
  +8      8     _M_pathname.length   (string length)
 +16     16     _M_pathname.union    (inline buf[16] or capacity)
 +32      8     _M_cmpts             (component storage)
──────
 40 bytes total

_M_pathname now stores its pointer, length, and either a 16-byte inline character buffer (for short strings ≤ 15 chars) or a heap capacity, all in 32 bytes, directly inside the path object.

The two layouts are not compatible. They disagree on the size of the object, the offset of every field after the first, and how std::string manages its memory internally. Code compiled against one layout cannot safely read or write an object created with the other.

The collision: reading 40 bytes from a 16-byte object

Here is the memory-level picture when the two ABIs collide. A shared library was compiled with the old ABI. It creates a std::filesystem::path object of 16 bytes. Your binary was compiled with the new ABI. It receives a pointer to that object and interprets it as a 40-byte struct.

What does the binary see?

Walking through each byte range:

Bytes 0–7 (_M_pathname.ptr): Both ABIs store a pointer at offset 0. The old ABI's COW pointer happens to point to a heap block where the character data eventually sits (after the length, capacity, and refcount fields). This is not identical to the new ABI's data pointer, but it's close enough that GDB can sometimes follow it and display the string content. Coincidental compatibility, not safety.

Bytes 8–15 (_M_pathname.length): The new-ABI consumer reads these 8 bytes as the string's length. But in the old-ABI object, bytes 8–15 are _M_cmpts, the component storage pointer or small-buffer state. A heap address interpreted as a string length produces a number in the trillions. Any code that uses this length to iterate over the string will read far past the end of any valid buffer.

Bytes 16–31 (_M_pathname.union): The consumer expects 16 bytes of inline string buffer or capacity here. But the old-ABI object is only 16 bytes long. These bytes don't belong to the path object at all. They are whatever happens to sit in adjacent memory: another local variable, alignment padding, freed heap metadata, part of a different object. The content is uncontrolled and unpredictable.

Bytes 32–39 (_M_cmpts): The consumer reads these 8 bytes as the component storage. Again, well outside the object. Pure garbage.

The binary is reading a 40-byte struct from a 16-byte region. The first 8 bytes are roughly compatible by accident. The next 8 bytes are wildly misinterpreted. And the final 24 bytes are whatever happened to be adjacent in memory.

What libstdc++.so expects

If the consumer calls a member function like parent_path(), the call doesn't stay inside the binary. parent_path() is implemented in libstdc++.so, the system's shared C++ standard library. That shared library was built with the new ABI. It expects every path object it receives to be 40 bytes laid out according to the new-ABI specification.

The call chain goes like this:

  1. Your binary passes a const path&, a pointer to what it believes is a 40-byte object
  2. libstdc++.so's parent_path() dereferences that pointer and reads the object's fields using new-ABI offsets
  3. It reads _M_pathname.length from offset +8 and gets a garbage value (it's actually the old-ABI _M_cmpts field)
  4. It reads _M_cmpts from offset +32 and gets garbage (24 bytes past the end of the real object)
  5. When it tries to use any of these values (iterating path components, reading the string, checking bounds), it dereferences invalid pointers or reads nonsensical lengths

The result is a SIGSEGV inside libstdc++.so, in a function that is perfectly correct. The function is doing exactly what it should: reading fields at their documented offsets. The problem is that the object it received was built to a different blueprint.

But in the real-world incident, the crash didn't require a method call. It came from something more fundamental: the destructor.

Why the destructor crashes

Even if you never call parent_path() or any other member function on the mismatched object, the destructor alone is enough to crash. Here's why.

C++ destroys class members in reverse declaration order. For std::filesystem::path, the members are:

class path {
    string_type _M_pathname;   // destroyed second
    _List       _M_cmpts;      // destroyed first
};

The destructor starts with _M_cmpts. In the new-ABI layout, _M_cmpts sits at offset +32. But the old-ABI object is only 16 bytes. Offset +32 is 16 bytes past the end of the object.

When the new-ABI destructor runs on the old-ABI object:

  1. It reads _M_cmpts at offset +32. This is outside the object — whatever sits in adjacent memory is interpreted as a unique_ptr<_Impl> (a pointer to the component list implementation)
  2. If that garbage value is non-null, the unique_ptr's destructor calls _Impl_deleter::operator() on it — dereferencing a garbage pointer
  3. SIGSEGV: the garbage pointer (in the real incident, 0x1a — a string length leaked from an adjacent COW control block) refers to unmapped memory

The destructor never even reaches _M_pathname. It crashes on the first member it tries to destroy.

If the garbage at offset +32 happened to be zero (null pointer), the unique_ptr destructor would skip the delete and proceed to _M_pathname.~basic_string(). That destructor has its own mismatch problem: its SSO check compares the data pointer (at offset +0) against the inline buffer address (at offset +16) to decide whether to call operator delete. The old-ABI COW pointer at offset +0 doesn't point to offset +16, so the destructor calls free() on the COW pointer — an interior pointer into a control block, not a valid free() argument. Either way, the program crashes.

This also explains why the crash is non-local: the old-ABI library that created the object runs perfectly fine. Its destructor would have cleaned up the 16-byte object correctly using the old-ABI layout. But if the object crosses the boundary and the new-ABI consumer's destructor runs instead, that destructor operates on a layout it doesn't understand. The fault is at the boundary, not in either side's code.

C++ types are not self-describing

The fundamental issue is that C++ objects carry no runtime metadata about their layout. A std::filesystem::path doesn't have a tag saying "I am 16 bytes" or "I am 40 bytes." The compiler bakes the layout into the consuming code, and the consuming code trusts that every object it receives matches that layout. There is no runtime check.

When two separately compiled binaries disagree on the layout, nothing catches the mismatch:

  • Not the compiler: it only sees one translation unit at a time, and each side compiles cleanly against its own version of the header
  • Not the linker: it checks symbol names, not type layouts. If the symbol crosses through C linkage or void*, the linker sees matching, undecorated symbols on both sides
  • Not the runtime: there is no layout metadata to compare. The pointer is dereferenced directly, using the baked-in offsets

This is why ABI mismatches are among the hardest bugs to find. The code is correct. The logic is correct. The types match in source. Everything compiles and links cleanly. And then a field access at the wrong offset segfaults, and the crash shows up inside libstdc++.so, in code you didn't write and can't easily debug.

The defense is straightforward but requires discipline: build everything in the dependency tree (your own code, your third-party libraries, your prebuilt packages) with the same compiler, the same ABI flags, and the same standard library version. When that invariant breaks, the result is a silent, delayed, non-local segfault with no warning from any tool in the normal build pipeline. The companion article walks through a real-world case of this happening and what we did to prevent it from recurring.

entry.title: The Static That Died Twice
entry.summary: A field report from debugging a double-free crash that only showed up after all tests had already passed.
entry.content:
A field report from debugging a "double free or corruption (!prev)" crash that only showed up after all tests had already passed.

The log that shouldn't exist

[==========] 24 tests from 1 test suite ran. (158 ms total)
[  PASSED  ] 24 tests.
double free or corruption (!prev)

Read that again. Every assertion passed. GoogleTest printed its green PASSED banner. And then, with no test left running, the process reached for a chunk of heap memory that had already been freed, and aborted with exit code 134 (SIGABRT). That was enough to make the Bazel test suite fail even though all tests had already passed.

There was no flaky assertion to blame, no obviously broken mock, not even a stack trace pointing at test code. Whatever was wrong lived after the tests were over, in the machinery almost nobody ever looks at: global static teardown.

This is the story of tracking that crash down to its actual cause: a single class-static object that, thanks to how the build was wired up, existed twice in the same process and got destroyed twice at exit.

TL;DR for the impatient

The same small "settings" library got linked into one test binary through two different routes: once built from source into a shared library, once as a prebuilt static archive baked directly into the executable. A mutable, exported class-static object inside that library therefore existed as two physical copies, yet the dynamic linker's symbol resolution silently collapsed both copies onto a single address. Both copies' constructors ran against that one address, and at shutdown both copies' destructors ran against it too, freeing the same allocator buffer twice. Nobody wrote a bug to cause this. It was an emergent property of the build graph.

Act 1: "It says PASSED, so why did CI go red?"

The first reaction to a failure like this is disbelief. Exit code 134 means SIGABRT, but every assertion in the test suite succeeded before it. The crash happens strictly after RUN_ALL_TESTS() has returned.

The instinctive first suspects were the usual ones: a use-after-free in test fixtures, a bad mock lifetime, maybe a threading issue at shutdown. All of those were ruled out quickly, because the crash reproduced identically as a single, deterministic, single-threaded test with nothing exotic in it. That's a strong signal you're not looking at "normal" memory corruption. You're looking at something structural.

Act 2: symbol table archaeology

The binary in question is built from a large, modular C++ codebase, using a Bazel-like build system. Buried in its dependency graph is a small "settings" library (call it SettingsEngine) used by dozens of other components to read configuration from JSON. SettingsEngine ships a helper class, DocumentReader, that keeps a "canonical empty document" around as a fallback value, backed by a small pooled allocator:

class DocumentReader {
public:
    static const Document& getEmptyDocument();

private:
    static Document s_emptyDoc;   // owns a pooled allocator internally
};

Nothing unusual there. This pattern exists in thousands of codebases. The next step was to stop guessing about test code and start reading the binary itself. nm on the test executable and on every shared library it loads, grepping for that static:

$ nm -CD ./test_binary            | grep s_emptyDoc
0000000000123456 B DocumentReader::s_emptyDoc

$ nm -CD libsettingsengine.so     | grep s_emptyDoc
0000000000034560 B DocumentReader::s_emptyDoc

Two hits. Both B (bss, meaning uninitialized/zero-initialized static storage), in two different binary images. That single observation reframed the whole investigation: this isn't a lifetime bug in test code, it's a duplicated global across a shared library and the executable that statically links the same source.

A quick pass with ldd and strings over the executable confirmed the suspicion further: the same header/source pair for DocumentReader had been compiled from two different physical locations on disk (once from the monorepo checkout, once from an unpacked vendored binary package) and both copies had made it into the final link.

Pulling on that thread led straight to the dependency graph, and the actual source of the duplication: two unrelated build modules each declared their own dependency on "the settings engine" (one on the source repository, one on a prebuilt binary release of the same library) and nothing in the build graph deduplicated them.

DocumentReader.cpp was being compiled twice, into two separate binary artifacts that both ended up loaded into the same process. That explains the two nm hits, but not yet why destroying one of them would corrupt the other. For that, the backtrace of the crash itself was next.

Act 3: the backtrace names the crime scene

With a debug build in hand, the crash itself pointed straight at the destructor:

#7  _int_free ()
#8  __GI___libc_free ()
#9  DocumentReader::~DocumentReader ()
      -> code inside the TEST EXECUTABLE itself
#10 __cxa_finalize (d=0x7ffff7dbd000)
#11 libsettingsengine.so
      -> destructor registration OWNED BY THE SHARED LIBRARY
#13 _dl_fini ()

That is a strange stack: the destructor body executing is the copy compiled into the executable, but it's being invoked from the exit machinery that belongs to the shared library. Two different modules, one function body, one call chain. That mismatch was the thread worth pulling.

Act 4: the conditional breakpoint that made it undeniable

At this point the working theory was: "there might be two objects being destroyed, and one of the destructions is invalid." To prove it, the fix was to stop looking at code and start looking at addresses, with a conditional breakpoint on the destructor, gated on the specific instance:

break DocumentReader::~DocumentReader if $rdi == &DocumentReader::s_emptyDoc
run

The result settled the question completely:

HIT #1  -- called from __run_exit_handlers   (executable's atexit chain)
HIT #2  -- called from __cxa_finalize of the .so (shared library's teardown)

double free or corruption (!prev)
Program received signal SIGABRT, Aborted.

TOTAL DESTRUCTOR CALLS ON THIS ADDRESS = 2

Both hits fired on the exact same address. Not two different objects at two different addresses, but the same object, destroyed twice, by two independent teardown mechanisms that both believed they owned it.

The mechanism: how two objects become one

This is the part that makes the bug genuinely interesting rather than "just a duplicate symbol." If the executable and the shared library really had two independent, isolated copies of s_emptyDoc, each would construct its own instance and destroy its own instance without any crash. The reason they instead collide on one address comes down to how position-independent shared libraries resolve global symbols.

Because the class-static has ordinary (exported) visibility and the shared library is compiled position-independent, every access to s_emptyDoc, even from the translation unit that defines it, goes through a level of indirection (the GOT), rather than a hard-coded address. This is required by the shared-library ABI: if some other module in the process were to override the symbol, all consumers, including the "owning" module, must observe the same, single, global definition. It's the exact mechanism that lets you override malloc process-wide with LD_PRELOAD.

When the same symbol name is exported by both the executable and a shared library, the loader's global symbol resolution has to pick one winner for the whole process, and the executable's own definition consistently wins over anything a shared library brings in. So both GOT entries end up pointing at address A, the executable's copy. Address B still physically exists (that's the second nm hit), but it's orphaned; nothing ever dereferences it through the normal symbol-based path.

Two independent modules each believe they own a private static object. Both constructed "their" instance. Both registered a teardown callback for "their" instance. But symbol resolution silently made both callbacks target the same memory, so the allocator's internal chunk pointer gets freed once by the executable's teardown and then freed again by the library's teardown. Classic double free, just arrived at through linkage rather than through application logic.

Why this is sneaky

  • Every individual test passes. The corruption only manifests during global teardown, which almost nobody single-steps through.
  • nm and ldd look "normal" at a glance. Duplicate symbols across a static archive and a shared object are common and usually harmless (each module just uses its own copy). It's only exported, mutable, class-static data that turns this into a landmine.
  • The bug isn't in any one team's code. DocumentReader is fine in isolation. The test helper library is fine in isolation. The production populator libraries are fine in isolation. The defect is an emergent property of a build graph in which two independent dependency edges resolve to different builds (source vs. prebuilt binary) of the same library.
  • The crash signature (double free or corruption (!prev)) points you toward "someone freed a pointer twice," which is true, but the actual bug is one level up: "someone constructed the same static object twice, from two different modules, without either module knowing about the other."

Fixing it

Two complementary fixes emerged:

  1. Collapse the build graph. Make sure only one dependency edge (source or prebuilt, never both) ever reaches a given library inside one binary. This is the real fix: it removes the duplicate compilation entirely, so there is only ever one definition to link and one object to construct/destroy.

  2. Harden the library against accidental double-linkage. Replace the class-static object with a function-local static inside an accessor function:

    const Document& DocumentReader::getEmptyDocument() {
    static Document emptyDoc{};   // constructed on first call, once
    return emptyDoc;
}

    A function-local static's initialization guard variable is itself subject to the same GOT-based symbol resolution, so even if the function body ends up duplicated across a shared library and an executable, only one guard variable is ever live at the shared address, so construction (and the __cxa_atexit registration that comes with it) happens exactly once, no matter how many times the containing library is accidentally linked into the same process. This doesn't fix the underlying build-graph duplication, but it makes the library itself immune to this entire class of crash.

Takeaways

  • If a process aborts with a memory-corruption signature strictly after tests report success, look at global/static teardown, not your test code.
  • nm/ldd across every loaded module is cheap and can immediately turn "a vague heap corruption" into "a duplicated symbol."
  • A conditional GDB breakpoint keyed on a specific address is the single most decisive tool for telling apart "two different objects" from "one object, destroyed twice."
  • Mutable, exported class-static objects are quietly dangerous in any codebase where the same library can plausibly be linked in more than one form (source vs. prebuilt, static vs. shared) into the same binary. Prefer function-local statics, or avoid mutable global state entirely.
  • Fixing the symptom in the library (function-local static) and fixing the root cause in the build graph (deduplicate the dependency) are both worth doing: one makes the crash impossible, the other makes the duplication itself go away.
